blocks.text: In that passage rash words and curses are compared with the wandering and circling sparrow and with the דרור. A. Schultens, in his Commentary on this passage, p. 345 ff., shows that the latter may not unreasonably be understood of the swallow, from a similar usage of the Arabs, who are accustomed to denote rash levity by this proverb: طارت عصافيره [ṭārat ʿaṣāfīruhu], his sparrows fly. With this agrees another: طارت خطاطيفه [ṭārat khaṭāṭīfuhu] his swallows fly, customarily used of an empty and rash babbler.

Merrick, in his notes on the passage, shows from Eustathius and Hesychius that it is not unusual among the Greeks either to put the word βωμου [bōmou], altar, sometimes for temple. Schnurrer, it is true, in his Animadversions on this passage (in the Dissertations Published Together, p. 162), rejects this interpretation on the ground that it cannot be demonstrated by examples that the Hebrews used the word מזבח in the same sense. To me, however, a synecdoche of this kind seems so natural to the poets of every nation that I would recognize it in our Hebrew poet even without the authority of examples.
Philo, On the Life of Moses, book 3, and 2 Par. II, 8.

The observation of ANT. DRIESSEN on this passage deserves to be added, from his Specimen of Observations in which Certain Passages of the Old Testament are Explained, Defended and Emended, with a preface by Nicol. Guil. Schroeder, Groningen 1774 (this dissertation is included in the Συλλογη [Syllogē] of Philological-Exegetical Dissertations Published by Various Authors and Defended under the Presidency of A. Schultens, I. I. Schultens and N. G. Schroeder, Leiden and Leeuwarden 1775, vol. 2, p. 1094 ff.): „It has already been observed by others that this passage refers to a custom accepted among ancient peoples, whereby animals dwelling in a sacred building, especially birds nesting in its walls or on the sides of the altars, were regarded as admitted into the protection of the Deity, so that it was sacrilege to harm them or drive them from their abode. Yet it will not be useless or unpleasant to compare an altogether similar passage from the Older Monuments of Arabia [edited by A. Schultens, Leiden 1740], Poem 1, where, just as the Psalmist celebrates the excellence of the holy place and the kindness of the Deity on the ground that even animals find a safe abode there, so Amru Ben Elharith extols the excellence of the Meccan sanctuary in a similar way: ونبكي لبيت ليس يوذي حمامة [wa-nabkī li-baytin laysa yūdhī ḥamāmatun] يظل دها امنا وفيه العصافر [yaẓallu dahā āminan wa-fīhi al-ʿaṣāfir] وفيه وحوش لا تراب انيسة [wa-fīhi wuḥūshun lā turābu anīsatun] انا خرجت منه فليست تغادم [anā kharajat minhu fa-laysat tughādim] And we weep for the sanctuary, whose dove is not harmed, which rejoices secure in its shade, and the sparrows there too; there also wild beasts that are not frightened, tame, even if they go out from it; and they inflict no harm. The reason why I thought it worthwhile to compare this poem with the sacred hymn is that the same animals occur in both, namely sparrows and doves. The celebrated Schultens dates this Arabic fragment to the age of Solomon. Moreover, the particle את in the words את מזבחותיך undoubtedly means at, beside, as often elsewhere.“ Thus Driessen. These remarks, though aptly made, contribute nothing to determining the meaning of the word דרור; for swallows could nest in the temple just as well as wood pigeons.
